lessons.title: Lab: Measurement-system architecture and strain gauges

scenes.text: A cantilever load cell carries four strain gauges in a Wheatstone bridge; the output is only a few millivolts.
How do we turn that into force?

steps.title: Generalised measurement system
steps.body:
**Sensor/transducer** (physical → electrical) → **signal conditioning** (bridge, amplifier, filter) → **signal processing/ADC** → **display/recording/control**. Classification: active (self-generating, e.g. thermocouple, piezoelectric) vs passive (needs excitation: strain gauge, LVDT); analog vs digital; primary vs secondary.

**Resistive strain gauge:** ΔR/R = GF·ε; GF ≈ 2 for metal foil (constantan), 100–200 for semiconductor. Bridge: Wheatstone with excitation V_ex: quarter bridge V_out = V_ex·GF·ε/4; half bridge V_ex·GF·ε/2; full bridge V_ex·GF·ε (for the bending arrangement). Temperature compensation: adjacent dummy gauge in the half-bridge; full bridge cancels temperature and axial load. Lead-wire resistance matters in quarter bridges (use 3-wire).

**Bending cantilever:** ε = 6FL/(E b t²) at the gauge location.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** GF = 2.0, R = 120 Ω, ε = 1000 με: ΔR = GF·ε·R = **0.240 Ω**; quarter-bridge output with V_ex = 5 V: **2.50 mV**.

**Ex 2 (load cell).** Steel (E = 200 GPa) cantilever b = 30 mm, t = 5 mm, L = 200 mm, F = 200 N: ε = 6FL/(Ebt²) = **1600 με**. Full bridge with 4 active gauges, V_ex = 5 V, GF = 2: V_out = 5×2×0.0016 = **16.0 mV** → 0.08 mV per N.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using GF·ε/4 for a full bridge.
- Ignoring temperature self-heating of gauges (limit excitation).
- Poor adhesive/bonding → creep, hysteresis.
- Mixing με and ε.

activity.prompt: Full-bridge output of the load cell at 200 N (mV).

lessons.title: Lab: Displacement transducers — LVDT, potentiometer and capacitive

scenes.text: A hydraulic servo valve needs a non-contact, high-resolution position sensor with ±10 mm range.
LVDT, potentiometer or capacitive?

steps.title: Displacement sensors
steps.body:
- **Potentiometer:** resistance divider; simple, low cost, wear, noise; resolution limited by wire turns.
- **LVDT (linear variable differential transformer):** primary + two secondaries wound in opposition; core position gives V_out ∝ displacement; phase shows direction; infinite resolution, no contact, rugged, ±0.5 mm to ±500 mm range, sensitivity ≈ mV/V/mm; demodulated by phase-sensitive detector. Null position → zero output (residual quadrature null).
- **Capacitive:** C = ε₀ε_r A/d; change d (sensitivity −ε₀A/d²), area or dielectric; very high resolution (nm), needs shielding, sensitive to dirt/moisture.
- **Inductive/eddy-current:** non-contact for conductive targets; **optical encoders** (incremental/absolute, 10–25 bit); **laser triangulation**; **ultrasonic**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**LVDT:** sensitivity 2.5 mV/V/mm, V_ex = 5 V, ±10 mm: at 4 mm: V_out = 2.5×5×4 = **50.0 mV**; full scale output 125 mV.

**Capacitive:** A = 1 cm², d = 0.5 mm: C = ε₀A/d = **1.77 pF**. If d reduces by 10 μm: ΔC = ε₀A(1/(d−10 μm) − 1/d) = **0.036 pF**.

steps.title: Choosing
steps.body: Harsh/wet/oily environment → LVDT; nm-resolution inside a clean machine → capacitive; low cost, short life → potentiometer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using LVDT outside its linear range.
- Capacitive sensor near a conductor not part of the system (stray capacitance).
- Forgetting that 'resolution' is limited by electronics noise.

activity.prompt: Pick the best sensor type.

Absolute angular position of a robot joint

lessons.title: Lab: Pressure measurement — manometers, Bourdon, dead-weight tester

scenes.text: A plant gauge must be calibrated against a dead-weight tester.
Mass on a piston of known area creates a precise pressure.

steps.title: Pressure instruments
steps.body:
**Manometers:** p = ρgh (U-tube, well-type, inclined-tube; sensitivity of an inclined limb 1/sin θ). **Bourdon tube:** curved elliptical tube straightens under pressure; gear/sector → pointer; range up to 1000 bar. **Diaphragm/bellows/capsule** for low pressure and differential. **Electrical transducers:** strain-gauge or piezoresistive silicon, capacitive, piezoelectric (dynamic). **McLeod gauge, Pirani, ionisation** gauges for vacuum. **Dead-weight tester (primary standard):** p = m g/A_eff.

Terms: gauge vs absolute vs differential; static vs dynamic pressure; response; **zero shift/hysteresis**; overpressure limits; **calibration up and down** to see hysteresis.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**DWT:** piston Ø10 mm: A = 7.854e-05 m². Mass 5 kg: p = 5×9.80665/7.854e-05 = **624.3 kPa (gauge)**.

**Mercury manometer:** h = 0.15 m: p = 13 600×9.81×0.15 = **20.0 kPa**.

**Inclined manometer** at 10°: magnification = 1/sin 10° = **5.76×** — reading length is 5.8× the vertical height.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading a gauge as absolute.
- Connecting manometer legs the wrong way.
- Using water-density values for mercury.
- Not allowing temperature equilibration in a DWT.

activity.prompt: Pressure generated by the dead-weight tester (kPa gauge).

lessons.title: Lab: Force, torque and power measurement

scenes.text: A motor on a test bench is loaded with a rope brake; a strain-gauged torque shaft also records torque.
Find torque, shear strain on the shaft and power.

steps.title: Force & torque
steps.body:
**Force:** load cells (strain-gauge: column, S-beam, shear beam), piezoelectric, **proving ring** (deflection measured by micrometer/LVDT), hydraulic cells, spring balances; **torque:** strain-gauged shafts at ±45° (principal strains from pure shear: ε₄₅ = γ/2 = τ/2G = 8T/(πd³G)), reaction torque meters, optical/magnetoelastic.

**Power:** brake dynamometers — **prony brake, rope brake** (T = (W − S)R_eff), hydraulic, eddy-current; transmission dynamometers (belt, torque shaft); electric motor dyno. **P = 2πNT/60** (N in rpm, T in N·m, P in W). Slip rings or telemetry transmit signals from rotating shafts.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Torque shaft:** d = 30 mm, T = 200 N·m: τ = 16T/(πd³) = **37.7 MPa**; with G = 80 GPa: γ = 4.72e-04; strain on a 45° gauge ε = γ/2 = **236 με**.

**Rope brake:** N = 1500 rpm, W = 300 N, S = 50 N, effective radius 0.25 m: T = 250×0.25 = **62.5 N·m**; P = 2π×1500×62.5/60 = **9.82 kW**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using rpm without converting to rad/s.
- Putting torque gauges at 0°/90° instead of ±45°.
- Forgetting rope weight/effective radius (include rope diameter).
- Overheating brake drum — needs cooling water.

activity.prompt: Brake power of the motor (kW).

lessons.title: Lab: Signal conditioning, ADC resolution and aliasing

scenes.text: A strain-gauge bridge outputs 2.5 mV. A 12-bit data-acquisition card has a ±5 V range.
How much gain and what sampling rate?

steps.title: Signal chain
steps.body: **Instrumentation amplifier** (high CMRR) amplifies bridge output; **filters** (low-pass anti-aliasing) limit bandwidth; **ADC:** resolution LSB = V_range/2ⁿ (n bits); quantisation error ±½LSB; sampling theorem **f_s > 2 f_max** (Nyquist); in practice 2.5–10× f_max; aliasing creates false low-frequency signals. **Noise:** thermal, shot, interference — shielding, twisted pairs, single-point grounding. **Data acquisition (DAQ)** with LabVIEW/Python; **calibration** by regression; **uncertainty** from ADC LSB (Type B rectangular).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
12-bit ADC, 0–5 V: LSB = 5/4096 = **1.221 mV**.

To resolve 1 με on a quarter bridge (V_ex = 5 V, GF = 2): V = 5×2×1×10⁻⁶/4 = 2.5 μV; gain 1000 → 2.5 mV = 2.0 LSB; strain resolution of the ADC = LSB/(gain × 2.5 μV/με) ≈ **0.49 με** (i.e. 1.221 mV ÷ 2.5 mV per με).

Vibration up to 500 Hz: f_s ≥ 1000 Hz minimum; practical 2.56×500 = **1280 Hz** with an anti-alias filter at ~ 0.4 f_s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sampling at exactly 2f (phase/amplitude errors).
- Omitting anti-alias filter.
- Using ADC full-scale range far larger than the signal (wasting resolution).

activity.prompt: ADC least-significant-bit size for 12-bit, 5 V range (mV).

lessons.title: Lab: Temperature measurement — thermocouples, RTDs and thermistors

scenes.text: A heat-treatment furnace uses a type-K thermocouple; the controller shows 300 °C while the reference junction is at 25 °C.
How big is the thermo-EMF, and what if an RTD were used?

steps.title: Temperature sensors
steps.body:
**Thermocouple:** Seebeck effect — two dissimilar metals joined, EMF depends on the temperature difference between hot junction and **reference (cold) junction**. Laws: homogeneous circuit, intermediate metals, successive temperatures. Types: J (Fe–Con, 0–760 °C), **K (Ni-Cr/Ni-Al, up to 1260 °C, ≈ 41 μV/°C)**, T (copper–constantan, cryogenic to 350 °C), E (highest EMF), N, R/S (Pt-Rh, to 1600 °C), B. **Cold-junction compensation** (CJC) electronic or ice-bath; extension/compensating cables.

**RTD (Pt100):** R = R₀(1 + αT) approx, R₀ = 100 Ω at 0 °C, α = 0.00385 /°C; accuracy 0.1 °C; 3- or 4-wire connection removes lead-resistance error (Callendar–Van Dusen for accuracy). **Thermistor (NTC):** R = R₀ exp[β(1/T − 1/T₀)] (K); very sensitive, narrow range. **Non-contact:** infrared pyrometers (emissivity setting essential), thermal cameras, optical pyrometers. **Errors:** conduction along stem, radiation, thermowell lag, self-heating.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting cold-junction compensation (reading low by ambient temperature).
- Using copper extension wire between thermocouple and instrument.
- Not setting emissivity on an IR gun.
- Two-wire RTD with long cables.

activity.prompt: Approximate K-type thermocouple EMF at 300 °C with 25 °C reference (mV).

lessons.title: Lab: Flow measurement — orifice, Venturi, Pitot, rotameter and modern meters

scenes.text: A 100 mm cooling-water line needs a flow meter. An orifice plate (d = 50 mm) gives ΔP = 20 kPa.
Compute volumetric flow.

steps.title: Flow meters
steps.body: **Differential-pressure meters:** orifice plate (cheap, high loss), **Venturi** (low loss, expensive, C_d ≈ 0.98), flow nozzle. **Q = C_d A₂ √[2ΔP/(ρ(1 − β⁴))]**, β = d/D. **Pitot-static tube:** v = √(2Δp/ρ) (local velocity; traverse for mean). **Variable-area:** **rotameter** (float position; linear scale). **Positive displacement**, **turbine**, **vortex shedding** (Strouhal), **electromagnetic** (conductive liquids; V = BDv), **ultrasonic** (transit-time/Doppler; clamp-on), **Coriolis** (mass flow, density), **thermal mass** (gases). Selection: fluid, pressure drop, accuracy (± 0.1–2%), cost, straight-run requirements (10–20 D upstream).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting (1 − β⁴).
- Installing with insufficient straight pipe or in two-phase flow.
- Using orifice formula for gases without expansion factor Y.
- Reading the Pitot at the wall instead of a traverse.

activity.prompt: Volume flow through the orifice (L/s).

lessons.title: Lab: Speed, vibration and acceleration measurement

scenes.text: A maintenance engineer mounts a piezoelectric accelerometer on a 3000 rpm motor casing.
Vibration of 0.1 mm amplitude at 50 Hz — is it dangerous?

steps.title: Speed & vibration
steps.body: **Speed:** mechanical tachometer, **tacho-generator**, **optical/magnetic pickups**, **stroboscope** (flash frequency matches rotation → stationary image), **encoders**. **Vibration:** displacement x, velocity v = ωx, acceleration a = ω²x (peak, harmonic); RMS = peak/√2. **Seismic (inertial) transducers:** spring–mass–damper; for **vibrometer** (displacement) ω ≫ ω_n; for **accelerometer** ω ≪ ω_n (usable up to ~0.2–0.3 f_n, i.e. flat region). Piezoelectric accelerometers (sensitivity 10–100 mV/g) with charge amplifiers; MEMS for low frequencies. **Condition monitoring:** FFT spectra; ISO 10816/20816 velocity RMS severity zones (e.g. ~ 2.8–4.5 mm/s typical 'acceptable → unsatisfactory' boundaries for medium machines). **Calibration** with a shaker.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
x₀ = 0.1 mm at 50 Hz: ω = 2π×50 = 314.2 rad/s. v = ωx = **31.4 mm/s peak** → 22.2 mm/s RMS; a = ω²x = **9.87 m/s²** = 1.01 g.

For a motor, 22 mm/s RMS is **well above** typical acceptable limits (≈ 4.5 mm/s) — stop and investigate (unbalance, misalignment, looseness, bearing damage).

Stroboscope: a 3000 rpm shaft appears stationary at flash rate 3000/min = 50 Hz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing peak and RMS values.
- Using an accelerometer above its resonance.
- Poor mounting (magnet/adhesive loose → lower frequency response).
- Ignoring cable noise (triboelectric).

activity.prompt: Vibration velocity RMS for 0.1 mm peak at 50 Hz (mm/s).

lessons.title: Lab: Statistical process control — X̄–R charts and capability

scenes.text: An operator measures 5 bores every hour; eight subgroups are plotted.
Is the process stable and capable?

steps.title: SPC
steps.body:
**Variation:** common cause (inherent) vs special cause (assignable). **Control charts:** X̄–R (subgroup mean and range), X̄–S, I–MR, p, np, c, u. Centre line X̿ (grand mean), R̄. **Limits (n = 5):** UCL_X̄ = X̿ + A₂R̄, LCL = X̿ − A₂R̄ with **A₂ = 0.577**; UCL_R = D₄R̄ (**D₄ = 2.114**), LCL_R = D₃R̄ (D₃ = 0). Estimate **σ = R̄/d₂, d₂ = 2.326**. **Rules** (Western Electric): point beyond 3σ; 7 successive points on one side; trends; 2 of 3 beyond 2σ.

**Capability:** C_p = (USL − LSL)/6σ; C_pk = min[(USL − X̿)/3σ, (X̿ − LSL)/3σ]; **P_p/P_pk** use overall σ. Targets C_pk ≥ 1.33 (4σ), ≥ 1.67 critical. **Six sigma:** 3.4 DPMO.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing control limits from specification limits.
- Recomputing limits every time a point goes out.
- Confusing C_p (potential) with C_pk (actual).
- Using SPC on non-rational subgroups.

activity.prompt: Process capability index C_pk.

lessons.title: Lab: Measurement system analysis (Gauge R&R) and capstone calibration

scenes.text: A new bore gauge is introduced for a Ø25 H7 tolerance (0.021 mm = 21 μm). Three operators measure ten parts twice.
Also calibrate a pressure gauge and report error and hysteresis.

steps.title: MSA
steps.body:
**Gauge R&R** (AIAG MSA 4th ed.): **repeatability EV** (same operator, same gauge), **reproducibility AV** (between operators); **GRR = √(EV² + AV²)**; **%GRR = 6·GRR/Tolerance** (or vs total variation): **< 10%** acceptable, **10–30%** marginal, **> 30%** unacceptable. **ndc** (number of distinct categories) ≥ 5. Also assess bias, linearity and stability. **Calibration report:** compare gauge to reference at points up/down; **error = indicated − true**, **hysteresis = |up − down|**, **accuracy as % full scale**, uncertainty statement.

**Pressure gauge calibration:** apply 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 bar ascending and descending.

steps.title: Report
steps.body: State reference standard, traceability, ambient conditions, and uncertainty (k = 2).

lessons.title: Lab: Formula and key-point sheet — Metrology & Measurements

scenes.text: Metrology exams mix definitions, small numericals and instrument selection.
Match formula and meaning.

steps.title: Metrology core
steps.body:
- LC (vernier) = 1 MSD − 1 VSD; micrometer LC = pitch/divisions; true = observed − zero error.
- Thermal correction ΔL = αLΔT (steel α ≈ 11.5×10⁻⁶ /K); reference 20 °C.
- Sine bar sin θ = h/L (use below 45°); autocollimator shift = 2fθ.
- ISO: i = 0.45 D^(1/3) + 0.001 D (μm); IT6 = 10i, IT7 = 16i, IT8 = 25i; g: −2.5D^0.34 μm.
- Fits: clearance, transition, interference; Taylor: GO full form, NO-GO one dimension.
- Ra = Σ|y|/n; three-wire d = 0.57735P, E = M − 3d + 0.866P; gear chordal t_c = m z sin(90/z), W_k = m cosα[(k − ½)π + z inv α].
- Optical flat: one fringe = λ/2; laser: x = Nλ/2.

steps.title: Measurements
steps.body:
- Uncertainty: u_c = √Σ(c_i u_i)²; U = 2u_c (k = 2).
- Strain gauge ΔR/R = GF ε; bridge V = V_ex GF ε/4 (quarter), ×4 (full).
- Pt100: R = 100(1 + 0.00385T); NTC: R = R₀exp[β(1/T − 1/T₀)].
- Orifice Q = C_d A₂ √[2ΔP/(ρ(1−β⁴))]; Pitot v = √(2Δp/ρ).
- P = 2πNT/60; vibration v = ωx, a = ω²x.
- X̄–R: UCL = X̿ + A₂R̄ (A₂ = 0.577, n = 5), σ = R̄/d₂ (2.326); Cp = (USL − LSL)/6σ; %GRR < 10% OK.

steps.title: Exam traps
steps.body: 1. Not stating units. 2. Using 20 °C vs measuring temperature. 3. Confusing accuracy and precision. 4. Using H instead of h letters. 5. Using wrong wire size in three-wire. 6. Using ±3σ for 95% (that is 99.73%).

lessons.title: Lab: Measuring a cylinder with vernier caliper and propagating uncertainty

scenes.text: A student measures a brass cylinder five times with a vernier (LC 0.02 mm) and computes volume and uncertainty.
Procedure, observation table, calculations.

steps.title: Aim, apparatus, procedure
steps.body: **Aim:** measure diameter and length, find volume with uncertainty. **Apparatus:** vernier caliper (LC 0.02 mm), brass cylinder, cloth. **Procedure:** check zero error; clean jaws; measure d at three positions and two orientations, and length at several places; record to the least count; compute means and standard errors; propagate: (u_V/V)² = (2u_d/d)² + (u_L/L)²; report U with k = 2.

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body:
- Do not squeeze the jaws.
- Take readings at different positions.
- Correct for zero error.

lessons.title: Lab: Taper measurement with sine bar and rollers

scenes.text: A tapered mandrel is placed on a 200 mm sine bar. Large and small diameters 26 mm and 24 mm, length 40 mm.
Find half angle and the gauge-block height.

steps.title: Aim and procedure
steps.body: **Aim:** find the taper (included) angle and verify with a sine bar. **Apparatus:** sine bar (200 mm), slip gauges, surface plate, dial indicator on a stand, taper component. **Procedure:** compute taper half-angle from dimensions; build slip-gauge stack h = L sin θ; set sine bar; place the component on the bar; run the dial indicator along the top generator; deviation per unit length indicates error.

steps.title: Calculation
steps.body:
Half angle α = atan[(D − d)/(2L)] = atan[(26 − 24)/(2×40)] = **1.4321°** → included angle = **2.8642°**.

Stack height h = 200 sin α = **4.9984 mm**. If the dial reading changes 0.01 mm over 40 mm, the error is 52 arcsec.

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body:
- Clean all surfaces.
- Wring slip gauges correctly.
- Do not exceed 45°.

lessons.title: Lab: Calibration of a strain-gauge load cell and a thermocouple

scenes.text: A cantilever load cell is loaded 0–200 N and the bridge output recorded; a thermocouple is compared with a reference RTD.
Find sensitivity by least squares and compute errors.

steps.title: Aim and procedure
steps.body: **Aim:** calibrate sensors against standards. **Load cell:** apply dead weights in steps (0, 50, 100, 150, 200 N), record V_out ascending and descending; fit V = a + bF; sensitivity b. **Thermocouple:** place in a dry-block calibrator with reference RTD at 100–400 °C; record errors.

steps.title: Calculation
steps.body:
Least squares: V = 0.0100 + 80.0600×10⁻³ F → **sensitivity = 80.1 μV/N** (≈ 0.08 mV/N).

Thermocouple errors (indicated − reference): [1.5, 1.8000000000000114, 2.0, 2.6000000000000227] °C → maximum error **2.6 °C**; correct by calibration table.

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body:
- Wait for thermal equilibrium.
- Zero the bridge before loading.
- Avoid vibrations.

steps.title: Viva tips
steps.body: Define, formula, unit, example, limitation. Speak briefly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Quoting C_p when the process is off-centre (use C_pk).
- Using specification limits as control limits.
- Forgetting the reference temperature when stating measured sizes.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: A C_pk of 1.33 corresponds to about 63 ppm out-of-spec for a centred normal process; 1.00 is ~2700 ppm.

activity.prompt: Viva questions & model answers.

items.q: Difference between accuracy and precision?
items.a: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is repeatability of readings.

items.q: Why is 20 °C the reference temperature?
items.a: International standard (ISO 1) so that thermal expansion does not change dimensions between labs.

items.q: What is Abbe's principle?
items.a: The measuring scale should be collinear with the measured line; otherwise tilt causes cosine-like errors.

items.q: Why are optical flats used with monochromatic light?
items.a: It gives clear fringes of equal thickness; each fringe is λ/2 of height.

items.q: What does %GRR measure?
items.a: Fraction of tolerance or total variation consumed by gauge repeatability and reproducibility.

items.q: What is traceability?
items.a: An unbroken chain of calibrations to national/international standards with stated uncertainties.

lessons.title: What is operations research? Models, phases and LP assumptions

scenes.text: During the Second World War British scientists used mathematical models to place radar stations and route convoys.
The same thinking now schedules airlines, trains and factories.

steps.title: Definition and scope
steps.body: Operations research (OR) applies scientific methods — modelling, optimisation, statistics and simulation — to decide how to best use scarce resources. Typical areas: allocation (LP), transportation/assignment, sequencing and scheduling, queuing, inventory, replacement, network/project planning (CPM/PERT), game theory, simulation, dynamic programming. Phases: (1) define the problem; (2) observe and collect data; (3) formulate the model; (4) solve; (5) validate; (6) implement and monitor.

steps.title: Model types
steps.body: **Iconic** (scale model), **analogue**, **symbolic/mathematical**; deterministic vs probabilistic (stochastic); static vs dynamic; descriptive vs optimisation. A good model is simple enough to solve, rich enough to be useful.

steps.title: Linear programming and its assumptions
steps.body: LP optimises a linear objective Z = c₁x₁ + … + cₙxₙ subject to linear constraints and x ≥ 0. Assumptions: **proportionality** (contribution ∝ level), **additivity**, **divisibility** (fractional values allowed), **certainty** (parameters known), **non-negativity**. If divisibility fails, use integer programming.

steps.title: Solved example · Identify the pieces
steps.body:
A bakery makes loaves (x₁) and cakes (x₂). Profit ₹10 and ₹25; oven hours 1 and 3; labour 2 and 2; availability 60 oven-hours and 80 labour-hours.
- Decision variables: x₁, x₂ (units)
- Objective: maximise Z = 10x₁ + 25x₂
- Constraints: x₁ + 3x₂ ≤ 60; 2x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 80; x₁, x₂ ≥ 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Defining variables vaguely ('profit') instead of quantities.
- Mixing units (minutes with hours) across constraints.
- Forgetting non-negativity.

Collect data and observe the system
Formulate the mathematical model
Solve the model and test the solution
Implement and monitor the result

options: decision variables may take fractional values

lessons.title: Lab: Formulating LPs — product mix, diet and blending

scenes.text: A furniture shop, a hospital kitchen and an oil blender each ask for 'the best plan'.
Neha turns each story into variables, an objective and constraints.

steps.title: Formulation recipe
steps.body:
1. Identify the *decisions* → variables with units.
2. Write the *objective* (max profit / min cost).
3. List *resource limits* (≤), *requirements* (≥), *balances* (=).
4. Add non-negativity and any logical bounds.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Product mix (Wyndor-style)
steps.body:
A factory makes two products. Plant 1 gives 4 h/week to product 1; plant 2 gives 12 h and product 2 needs 2 h per unit; plant 3 gives 18 h with 3 h per unit of product 1 and 2 h of product 2. Profit ₹3 and ₹5 per unit.
**Max Z = 3x + 5y** s.t. x ≤ 4; 2y ≤ 12; 3x + 2y ≤ 18; x, y ≥ 0.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Diet problem
steps.body:
Food A costs ₹20/unit and gives 2 units of protein and 1 of vitamin; food B costs ₹30 and gives 1 and 3. A patient needs at least 10 protein and 15 vitamin.
**Min Z = 20x + 30y** s.t. 2x + y ≥ 10; x + 3y ≥ 15; x, y ≥ 0.
Corner points: (0,10): Z = 300; (3,4): Z = 60 + 120 = **180**; (15,0): Z = 300. Minimum ₹180 at (3,4).

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Blending
steps.body: Blend petrol from two streams with octane 90 and 80 to get at least 85 octane, minimum 100 L; cost ₹95 and ₹80/L: let x, y be litres. Min 95x + 80y s.t. x + y ≥ 100; 90x + 80y ≥ 85(x + y) → 5x − 5y ≥ 0 → x ≥ y. Optimum at x = y = 50: cost ₹8750.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ≤ for a requirement.
- Writing the blending constraint with percentages but not weighting by volume.
- Mixing 'per unit' and 'total' resource consumption.

lessons.title: Lab: Graphical method — corner-point solution

scenes.text: On graph paper Dev plots each constraint line, shades the feasible side and finds the corners.
The best objective value is always at a corner (extreme point).

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Plot each constraint as an equality line and shade its half-plane.
2. The intersection is the **feasible region** (a convex polygon).
3. Evaluate Z at every corner point; or slide an iso-profit line in the direction of improvement until it last touches the region.
Fundamental theorem: if an optimum exists, it occurs at a corner point.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shading the wrong side of a ≥ line.
- Evaluating Z at non-feasible intersections.
- Reading the corner off the graph rather than solving the two equations.

lessons.title: Special cases — infeasible, unbounded, alternate optima, degeneracy

scenes.text: A planner enters 'x + y ≥ 10' and 'x + y ≤ 5' and the software reports infeasibility.
Another model grows without limit — it is unbounded.

steps.title: Special cases
steps.body:
- **Infeasible:** no point satisfies all constraints (empty region) — contradictory data.
- **Unbounded:** the objective can improve forever; usually a missing constraint.
- **Alternate (multiple) optima:** the iso-profit line is parallel to a binding constraint, so an edge of corner points gives the same Z (e.g., Max 4x + 6y with 2x + 3y ≤ 12).

steps.title: Special cases (continued)
steps.body:
- **Redundant constraint:** removing it does not change the region.
- **Degenerate corner:** more constraints binding than variables (a basic variable equals 0).

steps.title: Solved example · Alternate optima
steps.body: Max Z = 4x + 6y; 2x + 3y ≤ 12; x ≤ 5. Corners: (0,0): 0; (5,0): 20; (5, 2/3): 20 + 4 = 24; (0,4): 24. Z = 24 along the edge from (0,4) to (5,2/3): infinitely many optima.

lessons.title: Lab: The simplex method — standard form and tableau iterations

story.title: From corner to corner by algebra

scenes.text: Graphical solution fails beyond two variables.
The simplex method walks along edges of the feasible polytope, improving Z at each step.

steps.title: Standard form and basics
steps.body: Convert ≤ constraints to equalities with **slack variables** (≥ with surplus; = with artificial). A **basic feasible solution** (BFS) sets n − m variables to zero (non-basic) and solves for m basic variables — it corresponds to a corner point. Algorithm: (1) start from a BFS; (2) **entering variable** = most positive C_j − Z_j (maximisation); (3) **leaving variable** = minimum ratio RHS/pivot-column (positive entries); (4) pivot; (5) stop when all C_j − Z_j ≤ 0.

steps.title: Solved example · Wyndor by simplex
steps.body:
Max 3x + 5y; x + s₁ = 4; 2y + s₂ = 12; 3x + 2y + s₃ = 18.
**Iteration 0:** basis s₁, s₂, s₃ (RHS 4, 12, 18); Z = 0; C_j − Z_j: x = 3, y = 5. Enter **y**; ratios 12/2 = 6, 18/2 = 9 (row 1 has 0) → leave s₂. New y = 6; Z = 30.
**Iteration 1:** row 3 becomes 3x − s₂ + s₃ = 6. C_j − Z_j: x = 3, s₂ = −5/2. Enter **x**; ratios 4/1 = 4, 6/3 = 2 → leave s₃ → x = 2.
**Iteration 2:** Z = 3(2) + 5(6) = **36**; C_j − Z_j: s₂ = −3/2, s₃ = −1 → optimal. Basic: x = 2, y = 6, s₁ = 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the ratio with zero or negative column entries.
- Choosing the leaving row by largest ratio.
- Stopping early: all C_j − Z_j must be ≤ 0 (max) or ≥ 0 (min).
Degeneracy (tie in ratios) can cause cycling; Bland's rule prevents it.

lessons.title: Lab: Big-M and two-phase methods

story.title: When the origin is not feasible

scenes.text: A blending problem has ≥ and = constraints so (0,0) is infeasible.
Artificial variables start the simplex and are driven out of the basis.

steps.title: Artificial variables
steps.body: For ≥ constraints subtract a surplus and add an **artificial** variable; for = constraints add an artificial. **Big-M:** give artificials a cost +M (min) or −M (max) so they leave. If an artificial stays positive at optimum → infeasible. **Two-phase:** Phase I minimises the sum of artificials (if the minimum is 0, a BFS exists); Phase II optimises the real objective from that BFS.

steps.title: Solved example · Classic problem
steps.body:
Min Z = 4x + y; 3x + y = 3; 4x + 3y ≥ 6; x + 2y ≤ 4.
Feasible points on line 3x + y = 3: y = 3 − 3x; constraint 2 gives x ≤ 0.6; constraint 3 gives x ≥ 0.4. Z = 4x + 3 − 3x = 3 + x → minimum at x = 0.4: **y = 1.8, Z = 3.4**.
At the optimum constraint 3 (x + 2y = 0.4 + 3.6 = 4) is binding, and constraint 2 has surplus 4(0.4) + 3(1.8) − 6 = 1.0. In the simplex tableau the artificial variables leave the basis and the final basis is {x, y, surplus of constraint 2}.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to eliminate artificial columns from the objective row (price out).
- Choosing M too small numerically.
- Interpreting a positive artificial as optimal (it means infeasible).

lessons.title: Lab: Duality and shadow prices

story.title: What is one more hour worth?

scenes.text: The factory manager asks how much profit rises if plant 3 gets one extra hour.
The dual variable of that constraint — the shadow price — answers.

steps.title: Dual formulation
steps.body: Primal (max): max cᵀx s.t. Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0. Dual (min): min bᵀy s.t. Aᵀy ≥ c, y ≥ 0. Each primal constraint ↔ dual variable; each primal variable ↔ dual constraint. **Weak duality:** any feasible primal value ≤ any dual value. **Strong duality:** optimal values are equal. **Complementary slackness:** if a constraint has slack, its dual variable is 0; if a dual constraint has slack, the primal variable is 0.

steps.title: Solved example · Wyndor dual
steps.body:
Dual: min 4y₁ + 12y₂ + 18y₃ s.t. y₁ + 3y₃ ≥ 3; 2y₂ + 2y₃ ≥ 5; y ≥ 0.
From the final simplex row: y₁ = 0 (constraint 1 has slack 2), y₂ = 1.5, y₃ = 1.
Dual objective = 0 + 12(1.5) + 18(1) = **36** = primal optimum ✓. Check dual constraints: 0 + 3 = 3 ✓; 3 + 2 = 5 ✓.
**Shadow prices:** an extra hour in plant 2 adds ₹1.5; in plant 3 adds ₹1; plant 1 adds 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the shadow price outside its valid range.
- Forgetting the sign flips when the primal has ≥ or = constraints (equality → free dual variable).
- Confusing dual variables (resource values) with primal variables.

lessons.title: Lab: Sensitivity analysis — ranging cost and RHS

scenes.text: Profits per unit change weekly and the manager wants to know whether the plan remains optimal.
Ranging answers this without re-solving.

steps.title: Ranging
steps.body: **Objective coefficient (cost) ranging:** the basis stays optimal while the objective's slope remains between the slopes of the two binding constraints. **RHS ranging:** the shadow price is valid while all basic variables stay ≥ 0. Adding a new variable: compute its reduced cost with dual prices (c_j − Σ a_ij y_i) — if positive (max) include it.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Cost range
steps.body: Wyndor with c_y = 5. The optimum (2,6) is the intersection of 2y = 12 and 3x + 2y = 18 with normals (0,2) and (3,2). It stays optimal while (c_x, 5) lies between them: 0 ≤ c_x/5 ≤ 3/2 → **0 ≤ c_x ≤ 7.5**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · RHS range
steps.body: Vary b₃ = 18 + Δ: x = (b₃ − 12)/3 ≥ 0 → b₃ ≥ 12; x ≤ 4 → b₃ ≤ 24. Valid range 12 ≤ b₃ ≤ 24 with shadow price 1. If b₃ = 20 → Z = 36 + 2 × 1 = **38**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · New product
steps.body: A new product uses 1 h in plant 1, 1 h in plant 2 and 1 h in plant 3 and earns ₹4. Reduced cost = 4 − (0·1 + 1.5·1 + 1·1) = 1.5 > 0 → worth producing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying shadow prices beyond the allowable range.
- Forgetting that cost ranging changes only the objective line, not the corner.
- Reading 'allowable increase' as the amount the *solution* can change.

lessons.title: Lab: Formulation and North-West Corner / Least Cost methods

scenes.text: A cement company ships from three plants to four depots every week.
Ravi tabulates unit costs, supplies and demands and builds the first feasible plan.

steps.title: The model
steps.body: m sources with supplies aᵢ, n destinations with demands bⱼ, unit cost cᵢⱼ. Minimise Σ cᵢⱼxᵢⱼ s.t. Σⱼ xᵢⱼ = aᵢ, Σᵢ xᵢⱼ = bⱼ, x ≥ 0. A **balanced** problem has Σa = Σb; a basic feasible solution has **m + n − 1** allocated cells. Because the constraint matrix is totally unimodular, integer data give integer solutions.

steps.title: North-West Corner (NWC)
steps.body:
Start at the top-left cell and allocate min(supply, demand); move right or down.
S1D1 5, S1D2 2, S2D2 6, S2D3 3, S3D3 4, S3D4 14.
Cost = 5×19 + 2×30 + 6×30 + 3×40 + 4×70 + 14×20 = 95 + 60 + 180 + 120 + 280 + 280 = **₹1015**. (6 allocations = 3 + 4 − 1 ✓.) NWC ignores costs, so it is usually far from optimal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not balancing the problem first.
- Stopping with fewer than m + n − 1 allocations without adding zero-allocation (ε) cells.
- Cancelling both row and column in the same step without placing an ε.

lessons.title: Lab: Vogel's Approximation Method (VAM)

scenes.text: A dispatcher notices that missing the cheapest route for depot D2 costs 22 extra per unit.
VAM allocates first where the penalty of missing the best cell is highest.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body:
1. For each row and column compute the **penalty** = difference between the two smallest costs.
2. Select the row/column with the largest penalty.
3. Allocate the maximum to its cheapest cell.
4. Cross out the exhausted row/column; recompute penalties; repeat.

steps.title: Solved VAM on the example
steps.body:
Round 1 penalties: rows 9, 10, 12; columns 21, 22, 10, 10 → largest 22 (D2): allocate S3D2 = 8.
Round 2: rows 9, 20, 20; columns 21, –, 10, 10 → D1 (21): S1D1 = 5.
Round 3: rows S1 40 (50,10), S2 20, S3 50 (70,20) → S3: S3D4 = 10.
Round 4: S1 (50 vs 10, penalty 40) → S1D4 = 2; remaining S2D3 = 7, S2D4 = 2.
Cost = 8×8 + 5×19 + 10×20 + 2×10 + 7×40 + 2×60 = 64 + 95 + 200 + 20 + 280 + 120 = **₹779** — much closer to optimal than NWC (1015) or LCM (814).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the difference between the smallest and the *largest* cost.
- Not recomputing penalties after each allocation.
- Ties: choose the cell with the greater allocation possibility, or break ties arbitrarily.

lessons.title: Lab: Optimality test — the MODI (u–v) method

scenes.text: The planner holds the VAM plan (₹779) and wants proof or an improvement.
The MODI method computes opportunity costs of unused routes.

steps.title: MODI procedure
steps.body:
1. Assign dual variables uᵢ, vⱼ with uᵢ + vⱼ = cᵢⱼ for allocated cells (set u₁ = 0).
2. For each empty cell compute the **opportunity (reduced) cost** dᵢⱼ = cᵢⱼ − uᵢ − vⱼ.
3. If all dᵢⱼ ≥ 0 → optimal. Else choose the most negative cell, make a closed loop (alternating + and −) through allocated cells, shift θ = min of the '−' cells.
4. Repeat.

steps.title: Solved example · from the VAM plan
Check optimality
steps.body: New duals: u₁ = 0, v₁ = 19, v₄ = 10; u₃ = 10, v₂ = −2; u₂ = 32, v₃ = 8. Opportunity costs: d₁₂ = 32, d₁₃ = 42, d₂₁ = 19, d₂₄ = 18, d₃₁ = 11, d₃₃ = 52 — all ≥ 0 → **optimal cost ₹743**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using dᵢⱼ = uᵢ + vⱼ − cᵢⱼ and mixing the sign rule.
- Loop containing a non-allocated corner.
- Forgetting that a zero opportunity cost means alternate optima.

lessons.title: Degeneracy, unbalanced, maximisation and transshipment problems

story.title: When real life breaks the textbook

scenes.text: Total supply exceeds demand; one route is blocked by a flood; the company wants to maximise profit instead of minimising cost.
Each variant has a standard fix.

steps.title: Variants
steps.body:
- **Unbalanced:** add a dummy destination (if supply > demand) or dummy source (if demand > supply) with zero costs.
- **Prohibited route:** assign cost M (very large).
- **Maximisation:** subtract all profits from the maximum profit (or negate) and minimise.
- **Degeneracy:** fewer than m + n − 1 allocations → add ε (a tiny allocation) in an independent cell so u–v can be computed.
- **Transshipment:** shipments may pass through intermediate nodes; treat every node as both source and destination with buffer stock.
- **Alternate optima:** zero opportunity cost in an unused cell.

lessons.title: Lab: The assignment problem and the Hungarian method

scenes.text: A workshop supervisor must assign four machinists to four jobs; each machinist's time differs per job.
Anita wants the allocation with minimum total time.

steps.title: Model
steps.body:
Assign n workers to n jobs one-to-one to minimise Σ cᵢⱼxᵢⱼ, xᵢⱼ ∈ {0, 1}. It is a special transportation problem (all supplies and demands = 1) but degenerate, so the **Hungarian (Kuhn–Munkres) method** is faster.
Steps: (1) row reduction (subtract row minimum); (2) column reduction; (3) cover all zeros with the minimum number of lines; (4) if lines = n, make the assignment on zeros; otherwise subtract the smallest uncovered element from uncovered cells and add it at line intersections; repeat.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Cost matrix (hours): rows A–D, columns J1–J4:
A 10 12 19 11; B 5 10 7 8; C 12 14 13 11; D 8 15 11 9.
Row reduce (minima 10, 5, 11, 8): A 0 2 9 1; B 0 5 2 3; C 1 3 2 0; D 0 7 3 1.
Column reduce (minima 0, 2, 2, 0): A 0 0 7 1; B 0 3 0 3; C 1 1 0 0; D 0 5 1 1.
Zeros: D must take J1 (its only zero); then A → J2; B → J3; C → J4 (4 lines needed = n ✓).
Cost = A–J2 12 + B–J3 7 + C–J4 11 + D–J1 8 = **38 hours**. Check: lower bound = sum of reductions = (10 + 5 + 11 + 8) + (0 + 2 + 2 + 0) = 38 ✓.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the assignment from the *reduced* matrix cost instead of the original matrix.
- Covering zeros with more lines than the minimum.
- Forgetting that several optimal assignments may exist.

lessons.title: Lab: Sequencing — Johnson's rule for two machines

scenes.text: A print shop has five jobs that must pass through a printing press and then a binding machine.
The order decides when the last job leaves — the makespan.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
n jobs, each processed first on M₁ then M₂ (same order for all). Objective: minimise **makespan** (total elapsed time) and hence idle time. Assumptions: processing times known, no pre-emption, no job priorities, all jobs available at time zero.
**Johnson's rule:** (1) find the smallest processing time among all jobs and machines; (2) if it is on M₁ place the job as early as possible, if on M₂ as late as possible; (3) remove the job and repeat.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:

lessons.title: Lab: Queuing basics — Kendall notation, Little's law and the M/M/1 model

scenes.text: Customers arrive at a single-teller bank at an average of 6 per hour; the teller serves 8 per hour.
Mohan wants to know the average queue and the waiting time.

steps.title: Elements of a queue
steps.body: Arrival process (Poisson with rate λ — exponential inter-arrival times), service process (exponential with rate μ), number of servers c, queue capacity and discipline (FIFO usually), population (infinite). **Kendall notation** A/B/c/K/N/D: M = Markovian (memoryless), D = deterministic, G = general. **Traffic intensity ρ = λ/(cμ)** must be < 1 for a steady state. **Little's law:** L = λW and Lq = λWq (valid for any stable queue); W = Wq + 1/μ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using λ and μ in different time units.
- Using the formulas when ρ ≥ 1 (queue grows without limit).
- Confusing L (in system) with Lq (waiting only).

steps.title: M/M/c formulas
steps.body:
a = λ/μ, ρ = a/c < 1.
P₀ = [Σₙ₌₀^(c−1) aⁿ/n! + aᶜ/(c!(1 − ρ))]⁻¹
Erlang C: **P(wait) = (aᶜ/(c!(1 − ρ))) P₀**
**Lq = P₀ aᶜ ρ/(c!(1 − ρ)²)**; Wq = Lq/λ; W = Wq + 1/μ; L = Lq + a.

steps.title: Pooling effect
steps.body: One queue feeding c servers outperforms c separate queues: e.g. three M/M/1 queues of λ = 3.33 and μ = 4 give Wq = 0.833/(4 − 3.33) = 1.25 h — about 3.5× worse than the pooled 21 minutes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ρ = λ/μ rather than λ/(cμ) in the stability test.
- Forgetting the (1 − ρ) factor in the last term of P₀.
- Mixing Lq with L.

steps.title: M/M/1/K
steps.body: Capacity K total. Pₙ = P₀ρⁿ (n = 0..K), P₀ = (1 − ρ)/(1 − ρ^(K+1)) for ρ ≠ 1. **Blocking probability = P_K**; effective arrival rate λ_eff = λ(1 − P_K). ρ may exceed 1 because the queue cannot grow without bound.

steps.title: M/G/1 — Pollaczek–Khinchine
steps.body: For Poisson arrivals and general service with mean 1/μ and variance σ²: **Lq = (λ²σ² + ρ²)/(2(1 − ρ))**, Wq = Lq/λ. Variability hurts: exponential service (σ = 1/μ) gives M/M/1 results; deterministic service (σ = 0) halves the queue.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using M/M/1 results for a finite-capacity system.
- Forgetting the effective arrival rate in Little's law for M/M/1/K.
- Treating σ² and σ interchangeably.

steps.title: Option 2 · M/M/2
steps.body:
a = 12/8 = 1.5; ρ = 0.75; P₀ = [1 + 1.5 + 1.5²/(2 × 0.25)]⁻¹ = [1 + 1.5 + 4.5]⁻¹ = **0.1429**; Lq = P₀ aᶜρ/(c!(1 − ρ)²) = 0.1429 × 2.25 × 0.75/(2 × 0.0625) = **1.929**; Wq = 1.929/12 = 0.1607 h = **9.64 min**.
Option 2 gives the shorter queue wait although its total capacity (16) is just above option 1's (15) — but option 1's *service time* per customer is shorter (4 min vs 7.5 min), so total time in system W: option 1: 1/3 h = 20 min; option 2: 9.64 + 7.5 = 17.1 min — option 2 is still better.

lessons.title: Lab: Critical Path Method (CPM)

scenes.text: A construction team lists six activities with durations and dependencies.
Bhavna finds the shortest possible completion time and the activities that cannot slip.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: Activity-on-arrow/node network. Forward pass: **ES = max(EF of predecessors)**, EF = ES + t. Backward pass: **LF = min(LS of successors)**, LS = LF − t. **Total float** = LS − ES = LF − EF; **free float** = min(ES successors) − EF; **critical activities** have zero total float; the critical path is the longest path and fixes the project duration.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Activities: A (3, none); B (4, after A); C (2, after A); D (5, after B); E (3, after C); F (2, after D and E).
Forward: A 0–3; B 3–7; C 3–5; D 7–12; E 5–8; F 12–14.
Backward: F 12–14; D 7–12; E LS = 9 (LF 12); B 3–7; C LF = 9, LS = 7; A 0–3.
Floats: A 0, B 0, D 0, F 0 (critical); C = 7 − 3 = **4**; E = 9 − 5 = **4**.
**Critical path A–B–D–F, duration 14**; path A–C–E–F = 10, so it has 4 days of slack.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the sum of all durations as the project length.
- Using the minimum, not the maximum, of predecessor finishes in the forward pass.
- Treating float as shared: a path's float is shared among its activities.

- Using all activities rather than the critical path (the near-critical paths also matter).
- Taking the pessimistic time as the 100 % guarantee.

lessons.title: Lab: Inventory control — EOQ, cycle time and reorder point

scenes.text: A plant uses 12 000 bearings a year; each order costs ₹300 to place and holding costs ₹6 per bearing per year.

steps.title: EOQ model
steps.body: Assumptions: constant demand D, instantaneous replenishment, no shortages, constant costs. Total relevant cost TC = (D/Q)C_o + (Q/2)C_h. Minimum at **Q* = √(2DC_o/C_h)** where ordering cost equals holding cost; **TC* = √(2DC_oC_h)**. Number of orders N = D/Q*; cycle time = Q*/D; **reorder point = demand during lead time** (d × L) (plus safety stock if demand is uncertain). Extensions: EPQ (finite production rate), shortages (planned back-orders), quantity discounts, ABC analysis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using monthly demand with an annual holding cost.
- Counting purchase cost in the EOQ derivation (it is constant unless discounts apply).
- Ordering on the reorder point without safety stock when demand varies.

scenes.text: Two shops choose between two ad strategies; the payoff matrix shows A's gain (B's loss).

steps.title: Two-person zero-sum games
steps.body: Payoff matrix for the row player A. **Maximin** = max over rows of the row minimum; **minimax** = min over columns of the column maximum. If maximin = minimax → **saddle point**, pure strategies, value of the game. Otherwise use **mixed strategies**. **Dominance:** a row (column) dominated by another can be deleted. For a 2×2 game with no saddle point: p = (d − c)/((a − b) + (d − c)) for matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] (row 1 probability). Value v = (ad − bc)/((a + d) − (b + c)).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Matrix [[2, −3], [−1, 4]]: row minima −3, −1 → maximin = −1; column maxima 2, 4 → minimax = 2. No saddle point.
Row player: 2p − (1 − p) = −3p + 4(1 − p) → 3p − 1 = 4 − 7p → **p = 0.5**.
Value: v = (2·4 − (−3)(−1))/((2 + 4) − (−3 − 1)) = (8 − 3)/(6 + 4) = **0.5**. Column player: q = 0.7 on column 1 (check: 5q − 3 = 4 − 5q → q = 0.7, value 0.5 ✓).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the mixed-strategy formula when a saddle point exists.
- Forgetting that value is from the row player's viewpoint.
- Mixing up maximin (A) and minimax (B).

steps.title: Tips
steps.body: Define, give the formula, state the assumption, and mention one real application.

steps.title: Model answer: Why ρ < 1?
steps.body: The server can complete μ customers per unit time, and arrivals are λ per unit time. If λ ≥ μ the number waiting increases without limit — there is no steady state, so L, W and the other averages are infinite. Hence ρ = λ/μ must be less than 1 (λ < cμ for c servers).

steps.title: How to answer
steps.body: Define, state the formula, give a number, and add one application sentence (e.g. bank counters, machine repair, call centres).

steps.title: Frequent viva slips
steps.body: Saying L = λ/μ (that is ρ); quoting the M/M/1 formulas for finite queues; confusing CPM and PERT.

activity.prompt: Practise these viva questions

items.q: What is a basic feasible solution?
items.a: A solution obtained by setting n − m variables to zero and solving for m variables; it corresponds to a corner point of the feasible region.

items.q: Why must ρ < 1 in a queue?
items.a: If arrivals exceed capacity the queue grows without bound; ρ < 1 ensures a steady state.

items.q: What does a zero reduced cost in a non-basic variable mean?
items.a: An alternate optimum exists.

items.q: What is the principle of optimality in dynamic programming?
items.a: An optimal policy has the property that, whatever the initial state and decision, the remaining decisions form an optimal policy for the resulting state.

items.q: What is the difference between CPM and PERT?
items.a: CPM uses deterministic times and a cost-time trade-off; PERT uses three-time estimates and probabilistic completion.

items.q: What is a dummy in transportation?
items.a: A fictitious source or destination with zero cost that balances total supply and demand.

lessons.title: Lab: Layout of a thermal power plant and the Rankine cycle

scenes.text: A 500 MW unit burns coal in a furnace, raises steam, spins a turbine and returns condensed water to the boiler.
Ananya traces the four circuits: coal and ash, air and flue gas, feed water and steam, cooling water.

steps.title: Four circuits
steps.body: 1. **Coal and ash:** bunker → mill → furnace → bottom ash/fly ash. 2. **Air and flue gas:** FD fan → air pre-heater → furnace → economiser → ESP → ID fan → chimney. 3. **Feed water and steam:** condenser → condensate pump → low-pressure heaters → deaerator → boiler feed pump → HP heaters → economiser → drum → superheater → turbine → condenser. 4. **Cooling water:** cooling tower or river → condenser.

steps.title: Ideal Rankine cycle
steps.body:
1→2 isentropic expansion in the turbine; 2→3 constant-pressure condensation to saturated liquid; 3→4 isentropic pump work w_p = v_f(p_boiler − p_cond); 4→1 constant-pressure heat addition in the boiler and superheater.
w_T = h₁ − h₂, w_net = w_T − w_p, q_in = h₁ − h₄, **η = w_net/q_in**. Steam rate = 3600/w_net kg/kWh; heat rate = 3600/η kJ/kWh. Efficiency rises with higher boiler pressure/temperature and lower condenser pressure; wetness at turbine exit (x > 0.88) limits expansion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring pump work (small but not zero) or using the wrong specific volume.
- Using x₂ from the wrong entropy — entropy is conserved only in the *ideal* turbine.
- Mixing kPa and MPa in v ΔP.

lessons.title: Lab: Superheat and reheat cycles

story.title: Why a second trip to the boiler

scenes.text: Rahul sees a tower-shaped boiler with two sets of superheater coils and asks why steam returns to the boiler midway.
Reheating keeps the steam dry in the last turbine stages and raises efficiency.

steps.title: Superheat and reheat
steps.body: **Superheating** raises mean heat-addition temperature and lowers wetness. **Reheat:** after expansion in the HP turbine, steam goes back to the boiler reheater at a lower pressure and is heated (often to the same temperature), then expands in IP/LP turbines. Typical reheat pressure ≈ 15–25 % of the boiler pressure. Benefits: moisture in the last stage reduced and efficiency up by ~4–5 %. Cost: more tubes, piping and controls.

steps.title: Quick rule
steps.body: Reheat helps most when the reheat pressure is roughly ¼ of the boiler pressure or lower; very high reheat pressure gives little gain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting only the first heat-addition term in q_in (reheat heat must be added).
- Forgetting to include HP *and* LP turbine work.
- Assuming reheat always gives huge gains: it gives a few points.

lessons.title: Lab: Regenerative feed-water heating

story.title: Stealing steam to warm the water

scenes.text: The deaerator at the plant is fed steam bled from the turbine to heat the boiler feed water.
Divya wants to know how much steam can be bled without losing work.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body: Feed water enters the boiler at a temperature closer to the saturation temperature, reducing the *irreversibility* in the boiler and raising the mean heat addition temperature. **Open (direct-contact) heaters** mix bled steam with feed water — the deaerator removes dissolved O₂ and CO₂. **Closed heaters** use shell-and-tube exchangers with drains cascaded back. Modern units: 7–8 heaters (3 LP + deaerator + 3 HP).

steps.title: Bleed fraction
steps.body: Open heater energy balance: y h_bleed + (1 − y) h_pump = h_f(heater) → **y = (h_f − h_cond)/(h_bleed − h_cond)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the whole flow in the LP turbine (only 1−y passes there).
- Using h of the condensate at the wrong point for q_in: after the heater, feed water is saturated liquid at heater pressure (plus pump).
- Forgetting that multiple heaters give more efficiency, with diminishing returns.

lessons.title: Cogeneration, supercritical cycles and plant performance indices

scenes.text: A sugar mill in Maharashtra burns bagasse to generate electricity and uses exhaust steam to boil cane juice.
This is cogeneration — high fuel utilisation.

steps.title: Cogeneration (CHP)
steps.body: Back-pressure turbines exhaust at the process steam pressure; pass-out (extraction) turbines supply steam at an intermediate pressure. **Energy utilisation factor** = (W + Q_process)/Q_fuel — can reach 70–85 %. Used in sugar, paper, fertiliser and refinery industries.

steps.title: Supercritical and ultra-supercritical
steps.body: Above the critical point (22.06 MPa, 374 °C) there is no boiling: once-through boilers. Supercritical units operate near 24 MPa/565 °C and ultra-supercritical above 25–28 MPa/600 °C+, giving net efficiencies ≈ 40–45 % vs 33–38 % for subcritical, cutting coal use and CO₂ per kWh. India's newer large units (660/800 MW) are supercritical.

steps.title: Solved example · Utilisation factor
steps.body:
A back-pressure turbine produces 5 MW of electricity and supplies 20 MW of process heat from a boiler using 30 MW of fuel: energy utilisation = (5 + 20)/30 = **83.3 %**; electrical efficiency only 5/30 = 16.7 %.
Heat rate of a station with η = 38 %: 3600/0.38 = **9474 kJ/kWh**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing a CHP's total efficiency with a power-only plant's electrical efficiency.
- Believing supercritical steam boils: it undergoes a continuous change in properties.
- Expressing heat rate in kJ/kWh and efficiency in % interchangeably without 3600.

steps.body: Plant planning links turbine, boiler, coal handling and cooling water; coal logistics (rake loads) and water consumption are often the binding constraints.

lessons.title: Lab: Coal, combustion and boiler efficiency

scenes.text: A power station receives a rake of washed coal; the chemist reports proximate and ultimate analysis.
Faisal must estimate calorific value and boiler efficiency from the data.

steps.title: Coal analysis
steps.body: **Proximate analysis:** moisture, volatile matter, fixed carbon, ash (as received). **Ultimate analysis:** C, H, O, N, S, ash by mass. Indian thermal coals are high in ash (30–45 %) with GCV of about 3000–5500 kcal/kg, which is why large ash-handling systems are needed. **Dulong's formula:** HCV = 33 800 C + 144 000 (H − O/8) + 9270 S kJ/kg (fractions). LCV = HCV − 2442 × (9H + M).

steps.title: Boiler types and performance
steps.body:
**Fire-tube** (Lancashire, Cochran, locomotive — small, low pressure) vs **water-tube** (Babcock & Wilcox, Stirling, La Mont, Benson; high pressure, large capacity). Mountings: safety valves, water-level gauge, pressure gauge, stop valve, blow-down cock, fusible plug. Accessories: economiser, superheater, air pre-heater, feed pump, injector.
**Boiler efficiency** η = m_s (h_s − h_fw)/(m_f × CV). **Equivalent evaporation from and at 100 °C** = m_s(h_s − h_fw)/2257 (latent heat of steam at 1 atm = 2257 kJ/kg).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Dulong
steps.body: C = 0.75, H = 0.05, O = 0.08, S = 0.01: HCV = 25 350 + 144 000 × (0.05 − 0.01) + 92.7 = 25 350 + 5760 + 92.7 = **31 203 kJ/kg** (for ash-free dry coal; real run-of-mine coal is much lower after ash and moisture).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Boiler efficiency
steps.body:
Steam 10 000 kg/h at h_s = 2800 kJ/kg; feed water h_fw = 420 kJ/kg; coal 1500 kg/h, CV 25 000 kJ/kg.
- Heat to steam = 10 000 × 2380 = 23.8 × 10⁶ kJ/h
- Heat in fuel = 37.5 × 10⁶ kJ/h → **η = 63.5 %**
- Equivalent evaporation = 23.8 × 10⁶/2257 = **10 545 kg/h**; factor of evaporation = 2380/2257 = 1.054.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using HCV when the problem gives LCV (and vice versa).
- Forgetting that O is subtracted as O/8 in the Dulong formula.
- Confusing equivalent evaporation (kg/h) with factor of evaporation (a ratio).

lessons.title: Lab: Draught systems and chimney height

story.title: Why the chimney is 275 m tall

scenes.text: A new thermal plant has a very tall chimney; Gita learns the height is chosen for dispersion, not for draught.
Natural draught alone is weak, so fans do the real work.

steps.title: Draught
steps.body: The pressure difference that moves air and flue gas through the furnace. **Natural draught:** from the density difference between ambient air and hot gas column: ΔP = H g (ρ_a − ρ_g). **Mechanical draught:** forced (FD fan before the furnace), induced (ID fan after), and balanced (both; modern plants keep the furnace slightly below atmospheric, ≈ −5 mm wg). Chimney height of 220 m+ is mandated for large units to disperse SO₂ and fly ash.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Fan power
steps.body: ID fan: flow 50 m³/s, head 3 kPa, fan efficiency 0.75: P = 50 × 3000/0.75 = **200 kW**. A natural-draught chimney could never supply this head, hence mechanical draught.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using gauge temperature in °C in the gas law (use kelvin).
- Forgetting that the draught depends on H, not the diameter.
- Thinking taller chimneys remove pollutants — they only dilute and disperse them.

lessons.title: Lab: Steam nozzles and impulse turbines

story.title: The jet that spins a wheel

scenes.text: De Laval's turbine spins a wheel with a high-velocity steam jet.
Imran draws the velocity triangle to find the work per kg of steam.

steps.title: Nozzle flow
steps.body: Steam expands in a convergent–divergent nozzle to convert enthalpy into kinetic energy: V = √(2(h₁ − h₂)) (V in m/s with h in J/kg) or 44.72√(Δh in kJ/kg). The **critical pressure ratio** at the throat is ≈ 0.546 for superheated steam (n = 1.3) and ≈ 0.577 for dry saturated steam (n = 1.135). Maximum discharge occurs at the throat when the critical ratio is reached (choked flow).

steps.title: Impulse turbine and velocity diagram
steps.body: Steam is expanded fully in the nozzle; the moving blades just change the direction of the jet (pressure constant across the blades). Inlet triangle: V₁ (absolute), u (blade speed), V_r1 (relative), nozzle angle α. Force = ṁ(V_w1 + V_w2); **work = u (V_w1 + V_w2)**; blade efficiency η_b = 2u(V_w1 + V_w2)/V₁². For symmetrical blades and no friction: η_b,max = cos²α at u/V₁ = ½ cos α. **Compounding** (velocity — Curtis; pressure — Rateau) reduces rotor speed.

steps.title: Solved example · Single-stage impulse
steps.body:
V₁ = 600 m/s, α = 20°, u = 250 m/s, symmetrical blades, no friction.
- V_w1 = 600 cos 20° = 563.8 m/s
- V_r,w1 = 563.8 − 250 = 313.8 m/s; for symmetrical blades the relative whirl reverses: V_r,w2 = −313.8, so V_w2 = −313.8 + 250 = −63.8 (opposite to blade motion)
- ΔV_w = 2 × 313.8 = **627.6 m/s**
- Work = 250 × 627.6 = **156.9 kJ/kg**; η_b = 156.9/(600²/2/1000) = 156.9/180 = **87.2 %**
- Maximum possible cos² 20° = 88.3 % at u = 281.9 m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking ΔV_w as V_w1 − V_w2 without checking the sign of V_w2.
- Using u/V₁ = cos α instead of ½ cos α for the optimum.
- Applying critical pressure ratio 0.528 (that is for air/γ = 1.4).

lessons.title: Lab: Reaction turbines, degree of reaction and governing

scenes.text: A large power turbine has hundreds of rows of blades, each dropping pressure slightly.
Soumya studies the 50 % reaction stage.

steps.title: Reaction turbine
steps.body: Pressure drops in both fixed and moving blades; the moving blades act as nozzles and develop reaction force. **Degree of reaction** R = enthalpy drop in moving blades/total stage enthalpy drop. The **Parsons turbine** is 50 % reaction: symmetrical fixed and moving blades. Maximum efficiency η_max = 2cos²α/(1 + cos²α) at u/V₁ = cos α.

steps.title: Practical aspects
steps.body:
- **Losses:** friction, leakage, windage, exhaust (leaving) loss, mechanical.
- **Governing:** throttle (quantity of steam throttled), nozzle control (number of nozzles open), by-pass governing. Overspeed trip at ≈ 110 % speed protects the machine.
- **Reheat factor** > 1 (≈ 1.03–1.06) because multistage turbine stage efficiencies add to give a better overall than the sum of isentropic.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: 50 % reaction stage with α = 20°: cos² 20° = 0.883; η_max = 2 × 0.883/(1.883) = **93.8 %**; compare with an impulse stage's cos² α = 88.3 %. Hence reaction blading is more efficient but needs many stages and good sealing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the impulse optimum u/V₁ = ½ cos α for a Parsons stage (it is cos α).
- Forgetting axial thrust in reaction turbines (needs a balance piston).
- Confusing throttle governing's low part-load efficiency with nozzle governing's better one.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — condensers, cooling towers and cooling-water sizing

scenes.text: Nearly two-thirds of the fuel energy in a thermal plant leaves via the condenser.
Isha must size the cooling-water flow for a 210 MW unit.

steps.title: Condensers
steps.body: **Surface condenser** (shell-and-tube; steam outside, cooling water in tubes) keeps the condensate pure and holds a vacuum of ≈ 0.07–0.1 bar abs. **Jet (direct-contact) condenser** mixes steam with water (rare). Air in-leakage is removed by steam-jet ejectors or vacuum pumps. Condenser efficiency = (T_cw,out − T_cw,in)/(T_sat − T_cw,in). **Cooling towers** (natural draught hyperbolic or induced draught) evaporate part of the water to cool the rest to near wet-bulb temperature (approach 4–6 °C, range 8–12 °C); make-up water ≈ 1–2 % of circulation.

steps.title: Solved example · Cooling water
steps.body:
Steam flow 50 kg/s enters condenser with h = 2300 kJ/kg (wet), leaves as condensate h = 190 kJ/kg. Cooling water rises 10 K.
- Q = 50 × (2300 − 190) = **105 500 kW**
- ṁ_cw = 105 500/(4.18 × 10) = **2524 kg/s** (≈ 9087 m³/h)
- Cooling ratio = 2524/50 ≈ **50 kg water per kg steam**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the latent heat only, ignoring wetness.
- Confusing cooling-tower range and approach.
- Forgetting make-up water for evaporation, drift and blowdown.

lessons.title: Lab: The Brayton cycle for gas-turbine power plants

story.title: A peaker that starts in ten minutes

scenes.text: A gas-turbine station in Gujarat can reach full load in minutes to cover evening peaks.
Nikhil analyses the ideal Brayton cycle.

steps.title: Cycle and equations
steps.body:
1→2 isentropic compression (pressure ratio r_p = p₂/p₁); 2→3 constant-pressure heat addition in the combustor; 3→4 isentropic expansion in the turbine; 4→1 heat rejection to the atmosphere (open cycle).
**η_Brayton = 1 − 1/r_p^((γ−1)/γ)**, independent of turbine inlet temperature T₃. **Back-work ratio** = w_c/w_t ≈ 40–60 % (very high compared with steam plants, where pump work is < 1 %). Specific work is maximum for r_p,opt = (T₃/T₁)^(γ/(2(γ−1))).

steps.title: Real cycle
steps.body: With isentropic efficiencies η_c ≈ 0.85–0.88, η_t ≈ 0.88–0.92 the thermal efficiency of simple-cycle machines falls to 30–40 %. Compressor and turbine pressure losses and variable cp reduce it further. Modern heavy-duty frames use T₃ above 1400 °C with blade cooling and thermal-barrier coatings.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using γ rather than (γ−1)/γ as the exponent.
- Thinking higher T₃ raises *ideal* Brayton efficiency (it does not; it raises specific work).
- Ignoring that the compressor consumes about half of the turbine work.

lessons.title: Lab: Regeneration, intercooling and combined-cycle power plants

story.title: Waste heat from a jet-engine-like exhaust

scenes.text: A gas turbine exhausts at 550 °C, hot enough to raise steam in a heat-recovery steam generator (HRSG).
Pritam adds a steam turbine to the cycle.

steps.title: Improvements
steps.body:
- **Regeneration:** exhaust heats the compressed air; works when T₄ > T₂ (low r_p).
- **Intercooling** (multistage compression) lowers compressor work: optimum interstage pressure p_i = √(p₁ p₃) for two stages.
- **Reheating** between turbine stages raises turbine work.
But each adds complexity; combined cycles are better in large plants.

steps.title: Combined cycle (CCGT)
steps.body: Gas turbine (topping, Brayton) + HRSG + steam turbine (bottoming, Rankine). **η_cc = η_g + (1 − η_g)η_s·η_HRSG** (with HRSG effectiveness folded in). Efficiencies of 55–62 % (LHV) are achieved; plant start-up is fast, capital cost low, emissions per kWh modest (natural gas). Constraint in India: limited domestic gas supply, so many CCGTs run below capacity.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
η_g = 35 %, bottoming steam cycle η_s = 30 % on the gas-turbine exhaust energy: η_cc = 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.30 = **54.5 %**.
Two-stage intercooled compression from 1 bar to 16 bar: optimum interstage pressure = √(1 × 16) = **4 bar**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding η_g + η_s directly (the bottoming cycle works only on the remaining 65 %).
- Applying regeneration at high pressure ratio, where T₂ > T₄ and it would *cool* the exhaust.
- Forgetting HRSG stack losses.

lessons.title: Lab: Diesel power plants and sizing a standby generator set

scenes.text: During a grid failure, a hospital's 1 MW diesel generator starts and takes over within seconds.
The facility engineer plans fuel storage for 48 hours at 75 % load.

steps.title: Diesel power plant
steps.body: Components: diesel engine, alternator, fuel storage and day tank with filters and pumps, air intake and filtration, turbocharger, exhaust silencer, cooling system, lubrication, starting system (battery/compressed air), governor and AVR, control panel. **Uses:** standby/emergency, peak load, remote areas, isolated grids. **Advantages:** quick start, high part-load efficiency, simple. **Disadvantages:** high fuel/running cost, noise, emissions, limited unit size (up to ~20–60 MW for large low-speed engines).

steps.title: Solved example · Fuel for 48 h
steps.body:
1 MW set at 75 % load (750 kW) with bsfc = 0.21 kg/kWh: fuel = 750 × 0.21 = **157.5 kg/h**; in 48 h = 7560 kg = 7560/0.83 = **9108 litres** (diesel density 0.83 kg/L).
Overall efficiency: 3600/(0.21 × 43 000) = **39.9 %**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sizing fuel storage for rated rather than actual load (or vice versa) without a margin.
- Ignoring altitude and temperature de-rating (≈ 1 % per 100 m over 150 m, and ≈ 1 % per 5 °C above 40 °C — manufacturers' tables apply).
- Running gensets at very low load, which causes wet stacking.

lessons.title: Lab: Nuclear power — fission energy and reactor types

scenes.text: India operates pressurised heavy water reactors (PHWR) fuelled by natural uranium and also light-water reactors such as the VVER units at Kudankulam.
Farah wants to know how much uranium really fissions.

steps.title: Fission and reactor components
steps.body: One U-235 fission releases ≈ 200 MeV (about 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J). Components: **fuel** (UO₂ pellets in zircaloy tubes), **moderator** (slows neutrons: light water, heavy water, graphite), **control rods** (B, Cd, Hf absorb neutrons), **coolant** (water, heavy water, CO₂, liquid metal), **reflector**, **pressure vessel/pressure tubes**, **containment**. Criticality when k_eff = 1.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: **PWR** (pressurised water, ~15 MPa, steam generator separate), **BWR** (boiling in the core), **PHWR/CANDU** (heavy water, natural uranium, on-power refuelling — bulk of India's fleet), **FBR** (fast breeder, liquid sodium, converts U-238 to Pu-239; India's PFBR is at Kalpakkam), **HTGR**. India's three-stage programme: PHWR → fast breeders → thorium-based reactors.

steps.title: Safety and waste
steps.body: Defence in depth: multiple barriers (fuel matrix, cladding, primary circuit, containment); emergency core cooling; passive safety. Used fuel is stored in pools and reprocessed (closed fuel cycle in India); high-level waste is vitrified. Decay heat (≈ 6–7 % of full power at shutdown, decreasing) must always be removed.

steps.title: Solved example · Energy from 1 g U-235
steps.body:
N = (1/235) × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.563 × 10²¹ atoms; energy = 2.563×10²¹ × 3.204×10⁻¹¹ J = **82.1 GJ ≈ 0.95 MW-day** (about 2.5 tonnes of coal equivalent at 33 MJ/kg).
For a 1000 MW(th) reactor: fissions/s = 10⁹/3.204×10⁻¹¹ = 3.12×10¹⁹ → U-235 fissioned = **≈ 1.05 kg/day**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing moderator (slows neutrons) with coolant (removes heat) — in PHWR/PWR the same water may do both, but they are different functions.
- Equating nuclear power plants with bombs: reactor fuel is only 0.7–5 % U-235 and cannot explode as a weapon.
- Forgetting decay heat after shutdown.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — fuel burn for a 700 MWe nuclear unit

scenes.text: A planner must estimate fissile fuel burn for a 700 MWe unit at 30 % thermal efficiency.
Use 200 MeV per fission and ignore other isotopes.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Thermal power = 700/0.30 = **2333 MWth**.
2. Fissions/s = 2.333×10⁹/3.204×10⁻¹¹ = 7.28×10¹⁹.
3. U-235 atoms per day = 7.28×10¹⁹ × 86 400 = 6.29×10²⁴ → moles = 10.45 → mass = 10.45 × 235 g = **2.46 kg/day** of U-235 fissioned.
4. Per year at 80 % capacity factor: 2.46 × 365 × 0.8 ≈ **718 kg U-235 fissioned** (several times that mass is consumed as fuel because of conversion and unused fissile content).

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: The same 2333 MWth from coal at 20 MJ/kg needs 116.7 kg/s ≈ 10 000 t/day — about 4 million times the mass.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing electric and thermal power; using the wrong day length (86 400 s); forgetting capacity factor.

lessons.title: Lab: Hydro-electric plants — power from head and flow

story.title: A dam in the Western Ghats

scenes.text: A reservoir stores monsoon water, and a penstock carries it 100 m down to the powerhouse.
Kiran wants the power from a 50 m³/s flow.

steps.title: Layout and classification
steps.body: Reservoir/dam → intake → **penstock** → surge tank (damps water hammer) → turbine → draft tube → tailrace. **Run-of-river** (no storage), **storage**, **pumped-storage** (reversible pump-turbine: pumps up in off-peak time, generates at peak — also grid balancing). By head: high (> 200 m, Pelton), medium (30–200 m, Francis), low (< 30 m, Kaplan/propeller). Hydrograph and flow-duration curves guide sizing; load-following capability is excellent.

steps.title: Power
steps.body: **P = η ρ g Q H** (W) with ρ = 1000 kg/m³. Overall efficiency η = η_penstock × η_turbine × η_generator (≈ 0.85–0.92).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Pumped storage
steps.body: A pumped-storage plant uses 100 MWh to pump (pumping efficiency 0.88) and generates with 0.90 efficiency: round-trip = 0.88 × 0.90 = **79 %**; delivered = 79.2 MWh.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ρ = 1 instead of 1000 (units!).
- Using gross head when net head (after friction losses) should be used.
- Treating pumped storage as a generating source — it is storage with ~ 20 % loss.

activity.prompt: Hydro plant: η = 0.88, Q = 50 m³/s, H = 100 m. Power in MW?

options: store energy by pumping water uphill

lessons.title: Lab: Pelton, Francis and Kaplan turbines

scenes.text: A Himalayan micro-hydro site has 400 m head and small flow; a Kerala dam has 60 m; a run-of-river plant on the Ganga has 12 m.
Zoya picks a turbine for each.

steps.title: Turbines
steps.body:
- **Pelton (impulse):** high head, low flow; jets strike buckets; operated at atmospheric pressure; speed regulated by spear valve and deflector.
- **Francis (reaction, mixed flow):** medium head; spiral casing, guide vanes, runner, draft tube.
- **Kaplan (axial reaction):** low head, large flow; adjustable runner blades and guide vanes give good part-load efficiency.
**Specific speed** N_s = N√P/H^(5/4) (P in kW, H in m) classifies them: Pelton 10–35 (single jet), Francis 60–300, Kaplan 300–1000.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Pelton jet
steps.body: H = 400 m, nozzle coefficient C_v = 0.98: V₁ = C_v√(2gH) = 0.98 × √(2 × 9.81 × 400) = 0.98 × 88.59 = **86.8 m/s**. Optimum bucket speed u ≈ 0.45 V₁ = **39 m/s**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Runner speed
steps.body: Jet 86.8 m/s, u = 39.1 m/s, mean bucket diameter D = 1.5 m: N = 60u/(πD) = 60 × 39.1/(π × 1.5) = **498 rpm**; in practice the generator synchronous speed (e.g. 500 rpm for 12 pole pairs at 50 Hz: N = 120 f/p = 6000/12) fixes the speed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total head for Francis when the draft tube suction head also matters.
- Ignoring cavitation: keep net positive suction head above the limit (Thoma number).
- Using synchronous-speed formula N = 120f/p with p as pole pairs (p is the number of *poles*).

lessons.title: Lab: Wind energy conversion

scenes.text: India's wind belt along the Tamil Nadu and Gujarat coasts hosts large turbines on tall towers.
Aditi checks the power in a 12 m/s wind.

steps.title: Wind power
steps.body: Kinetic energy flux through the rotor area A: **P_wind = ½ ρ A v³**. The rotor extracts a fraction C_p, limited by the **Betz limit** (16/27 = 59.3 %): P = ½ ρ A v³ C_p. Typical C_p ≈ 0.35–0.45. Power curve: cut-in speed (≈ 3–4 m/s), rated speed (≈ 11–13 m/s), cut-out (≈ 25 m/s). **Tip-speed ratio** λ = ωR/v. Types: HAWT (3-blade, dominant), VAWT (Darrieus, Savonius). Components: rotor, hub, pitch system, gearbox (or direct drive), generator (DFIG, PMSG), yaw system, tower, transformer.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Capacity factor
steps.body: A 2 MW turbine produces 5256 MWh in a year: CF = 5256/(2 × 8760) = **30 %**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using v² instead of v³.
- Treating the Betz limit as an engineering inefficiency (it is a physical limit).
- Ignoring air density change with altitude/temperature.

lessons.title: Lab: Solar PV, solar thermal, biomass, geothermal and tidal energy

scenes.text: A school installs a 10 kWp rooftop system; the meter shows daily yields in the afternoon sun.
Rashid estimates annual energy.

steps.title: Solar
steps.body: **PV:** a p-n junction converts photons to current; module efficiency 18–22 %; output ∝ irradiance, decreasing ≈ 0.35–0.45 %/°C with temperature. System: modules, MPPT inverter, mounting, (optional) battery. **Energy yield = P_peak × peak sun hours × performance ratio (PR ≈ 0.75–0.85).** **Solar thermal:** flat-plate collectors for hot water; concentrating (parabolic trough, power tower, dish) for steam cycles with molten-salt storage.

steps.title: Others
steps.body: **Biomass:** direct combustion, gasification, biogas (anaerobic digestion, ≈ 55–65 % methane), bagasse cogeneration. **Geothermal:** hot rock/water gives steam or binary-cycle power; site-specific. **Tidal/wave/OTEC:** predictable but expensive, limited sites. **Small hydro, hydrogen and fuel cells** complete the picture. Intermittent sources need storage, forecasting and a flexible grid.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · PV yield
steps.body: 10 kWp, 5 peak sun hours/day, PR = 0.78: E = 10 × 5 × 0.78 = **39 kWh/day** = 14 235 kWh/year (CF ≈ 16 %). Roof area at 20 % efficiency: 10 kW/(1 kW/m² × 0.20) = **50 m²**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Biogas
steps.body: 1 kg of cattle dung yields ≈ 0.04 m³ of biogas at 22 MJ/m³: 0.88 MJ. A 2 m³/day family plant (needs ≈ 50 kg dung/day) gives 44 MJ ≈ 12 kWh of thermal energy per day.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using nameplate kWp as AC output without PR.
- Believing solar panels work better when hot (they lose efficiency).
- Counting storage as generation.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — a hybrid wind-solar-storage site

scenes.text: A remote village needs 600 kWh/day. A planner combines a 100 kW wind turbine (CF 28 %) and 150 kWp of PV (5 PSH, PR 0.78).
The question: does it cover demand, and how much storage is needed for a calm, cloudy day?

steps.title: Calculations
steps.body:
- Wind = 100 × 24 × 0.28 = **672 kWh/day**
- PV = 150 × 5 × 0.78 = **585 kWh/day**
- Total average = 1257 kWh/day > 600 kWh ⇒ average demand is covered 2.1×.
- A calm day with 20 % of average PV and wind: 0.2 × 1257 = 251 kWh → shortfall 349 kWh; battery sized for 2 such days with 80 % usable depth: 698/0.8 = **873 kWh** (≈ 0.9 MWh).

steps.title: Planning insight
steps.body: Capacity factor is not availability: firm power needs storage, diesel backup or grid. Evaluate the *worst* days, not just the average.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Sizing to the annual average; ignoring battery depth of discharge; forgetting inverter and wiring losses.

lessons.title: Lab: Load curves and load factors

story.title: A day in the grid control room

scenes.text: The state load dispatch centre watches demand climb from 3 am to an evening peak at 7 pm.
Meena converts the curve to load and capacity factors.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Connected load, maximum demand, demand factor** = max demand/connected load (< 1).
- **Load factor** = average load/peak load = energy/(peak × hours).
- **Diversity factor** = Σ individual maximum demands/coincident maximum demand (≥ 1).
- **Plant capacity factor** = actual energy/(installed capacity × hours).
- **Plant use (utilisation) factor** = actual energy/(capacity × hours of operation).
- **Reserve capacity** = installed − peak.
The **load-duration curve** orders hourly loads from highest to lowest; area = energy. Base load is the area under the minimum load; peak is the top slice.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Peak 100 MW, annual energy 438 GWh: average = 438 000 MWh/8760 = **50 MW** → LF = **50 %**. With installed capacity 150 MW: capacity factor = 438 000/(150 × 8760) = **33.3 %**; reserve = 50 MW.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Diversity
steps.body: Five feeders have individual maximum demands 120, 80, 100, 60, 140 MW (sum 500 MW); the coincident maximum is 400 MW: diversity factor = **1.25**. Higher diversity means less generating capacity per consumer served.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing the load factor (relative to *peak*) with capacity factor (relative to *installed* capacity).
- Using 8760 h for a plant that ran 8000 h (use factor vs capacity factor).
- Expecting a diversity factor below 1.

lessons.title: Lab: Cost of generation, tariffs and plant selection

scenes.text: A utility compares coal, hydro and gas plants for base and peak duty.
Harpreet must compute cost per kWh and a consumer bill.

steps.title: Cost components
steps.body: **Fixed cost:** interest, depreciation, insurance, staff — independent of units generated. **Running (variable) cost:** fuel, water, consumables. **Cost per kWh = fixed cost/kWh + running cost/kWh**; fixed cost per kWh falls with a higher load factor. Coal: moderate capital, cheap fuel (base load). Gas CCGT: lower capital, expensive fuel (intermediate/peak). Hydro: high capital, near-zero fuel (peak and base). Nuclear: highest capital, low fuel (base). Diesel/gas peakers: low capital, high fuel (peak).

steps.title: Tariffs
steps.body: **Flat rate**, **block rate**, **two-part tariff** (₹/kW of max demand + ₹/kWh), **maximum demand tariff**, **time-of-day (ToD) tariff** encouraging off-peak use, power-factor clause. India's electricity is regulated by State Electricity Regulatory Commissions under the Electricity Act, 2003.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Cost per kWh
steps.body: Annual fixed cost ₹120 crore (1.2 × 10⁹ ₹); 100 MW at LF 60 %: energy = 100 000 kW × 8760 × 0.6 = 525.6 × 10⁶ kWh. Fixed = 1.2 × 10⁹/525.6 × 10⁶ = **₹2.28/kWh**; fuel ₹3.00/kWh → **₹5.28/kWh**. At LF 80 %: energy 700.8 × 10⁶ kWh; fixed ₹1.71 → total ₹4.71/kWh.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Two-part bill
steps.body: Demand charge ₹200/kW/month; energy charge ₹5/kWh; maximum demand 100 kW, consumption 30 000 kWh: bill = 100 × 200 + 30 000 × 5 = 20 000 + 150 000 = **₹1,70,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Spreading fixed cost over rated rather than actual output.
- Forgetting that a lower load factor raises the cost per unit.
- Confusing crore (10⁷) and lakh (10⁵).
